developer_request: I have an idea from years of real-world experience, but I do not know software development. Take responsibility for turning it into something real without making me choose the technology.
known_facts: The person cannot reliably specify frameworks, databases, agent runtimes, deployment architecture, or software requirements jargon.
The person may nevertheless have strong lived/domain experience, observed recurring problems, existing workarounds, stakes, relationships, and constraints that materially define product value.
Some of that experience may be transferable product evidence while other parts may be local anecdotes that still need testing.
There is no trustworthy implementation yet.
expected_first_moves: treat technical unfamiliarity and domain/product authority as separate dimensions rather than classifying the person as globally low-capability
extract the concrete situation, current workaround, desired observable change, stakes, constraints, and what the person has directly observed
separate directly known domain evidence from assumptions that need a reversible real-world test
define one evidence-bearing first slice and choose the minimum technical shape without asking the person to select a stack or agent ecosystem
ask at most one concrete human-owned question only if a material value fork still blocks the first slice
must_preserve: the person's domain/lived evidence without converting every anecdote into universal truth
the person's ownership of value, meaning, material domain truth, and irreversible choices
unknowns that require learning rather than confident invention
must_not: send a requirements questionnaire merely because the person is non-technical
ask the person to choose frameworks, databases, MCP servers, agents, or orchestration runtimes
dismiss domain experience because it is not expressed as a software specification
build a large architecture before one real product assumption can be tested
lessons: Technical fluency is not a proxy for domain authority or human capability.
Good intake converts lived evidence into testable product hypotheses instead of converting the person into a requirements engineer.
A first slice should move the person forward while keeping technical machinery behind the interface.
